title: The rababis
hookLine: Muslim musicians descended from Mardana's tradition sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir for generations

lines: A RABAB: SKIN, WOOD, LOW STRINGS.
cards: A wooden instrument with a rounded belly, a skin face, and strings that buzz low under a singing voice. That's a rabab.
In the janamsakhi stories, Guru Nanak sings and a Muslim companion named Mardana plays a rabab beside him, village after village, road after road. This path first met him on day thirty-one.
Tradition says Mardana's music didn't end with Mardana.
Families of Muslim musicians kept the craft, and for generations they sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir in Amritsar, until the partition of Punjab drew a border through their lives.

teach.b: First, the name. A rababi is simply a rabab player, and the word became the name for these families of Muslim kirtan singers. They sang Sikh scripture in the ragas it's written in, a calling passed from parent to child.

teach.h: SATTA AND BALWAND: INSIDE THE BOOK.
teach.b: Second, a place inside the book. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a ballad credited to two minstrels, Satta and Balwand, in Raag Ramkali, praising the Gurus and the light passing from one Guru to the next.
Tradition remembers them as musicians at the Gurus' court. So some of the musicians' own words sit inside the scripture, sung in gurdwaras today.
Third, what the border did. As rababi families remember it, when Punjab was divided they went west, to the new Pakistan, and the music they had carried into the Harmandir went with them.
Their kind of kirtan was heard less and less on the Amritsar side.
Some Sikhs speak of that as a real loss, and some musicians, Sikh and Muslim, have worked to bring the rabab back into kirtan. Fourth, the shape of the whole story.
A Guru walks the roads with a Muslim friend and an instrument.
The friend's heirs, Muslims too, keep singing the Guru's words for generations at the Harmandir.
Nobody in that story had to stop being who they were to sing together: a faith whose hymns, in its own stories, were carried on a Muslim musician's strings.

how: Kirtan in gurdwaras is usually led by Sikh raagis today; a small number of musicians, Sikh and Muslim, keep rabab playing and the rababi way of singing alive in performance and recordings.

practice: If you can, play a recording of the rabab, or of kirtan sung with one; if not, recall any low, plucked string you've ever heard.
Listen for the place where the instrument and the voice lean on each other, and think of who stands behind the sound: the player, their teacher, and their teacher's teacher.

wordCard.voice: Rababi. A rabab player: the name for the families of Muslim musicians who, tradition says, sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir for generations. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: one who plays the rabab, the name of the Muslim kirtan families.
